title: Programming Languages & IDEs

findings.claim: Compiler advantages include: 'source code is hidden'
findings.location: Key Fact box after 'Compiler vs Interpreter' collapsible
findings.notes: Technically correct — distributing only the compiled binary does obscure source code — but 'hidden' is a simplification; decompilation is possible. Appropriate for GCSE level.

findings.claim: An interpreter 'stops at the first error found. No executable file is produced'
findings.notes: Confirmed by Wikipedia (Interpreter computing) and GCSE GURU. Stopping at the first encountered error and producing no standalone executable are standard descriptors for interpreters in GCSE CS.

findings.claim: Assembly language uses mnemonics like ADD, MOV, SUB; translated by an assembler
findings.notes: Standard OCR J277 content. Confirmed by OCR spec section 2.5 delivery guide.

overall_quality: PASS — no significant factual errors. All compiler/interpreter/IDE descriptions are accurate for OCR J277 GCSE level.

title: Embedded Systems

findings.claim: A typical modern car contains over 100 embedded systems
findings.notes: IEEE Spectrum (2010) reports low-end cars have 30–50 ECUs; mid-range cars approach 100; luxury models (Volvo XC90, BMW 7-series) reach 100–150+. Citing 'over 100' as typical is inflated. A more accurate statement would be 'between 30 and over 100 depending on the model, with high-end cars exceeding 150.' Not a fabrication but misleading for a student who owns a modest family car.

findings.claim: Embedded systems run their program from ROM and typically cannot be reprogrammed by the user
findings.notes: Broadly correct for the GCSE syllabus. Modern embedded systems may use flash memory rather than mask ROM, but ROM/Flash is the standard GCSE abstraction and is appropriate here.

overall_quality: MINOR ISSUE — 'over 100' ECUs as typical is an overclaim. LOW-end cars have 30–50. The fact is not fabricated but could mislead students.

title: The Work of Others

findings.claim: Philippe Starck's Juicy Salif citrus squeezer for Alessi (1990)
findings.notes: MoMA's permanent collection catalogue dates the Juicy Salif as 1988 (the design/conception year). Wikipedia's dedicated Juicy Salif article gives 1990 (typically the year of commercial release). Britannica and the Philippe Starck Wikipedia article give 1987. The lesson uses 1990, which is defensible as the production/retail year, but MoMA's 1988 is the most widely cited institutional date. Not a HIGH-severity error since 1990 aligns with the Wikipedia article, but it conflicts with MoMA and Britannica. Consider changing to 1988/1990 or adding a note.

findings.claim: Philippe Starck's Louis Ghost Chair (2002), made from transparent polycarbonate
findings.verdict: YEAR INCORRECT — SHOULD BE ~2002 IS DISPUTED
findings.notes: Britannica explicitly gives the design year as 2000; Wikipedia's Philippe Starck article also states 2000. The chair was produced for Kartell. The lesson cites 2002, which is 2 years late according to the most authoritative sources. The material (polycarbonate) is correct. Severity: MEDIUM — wrong by 2 years on a key named design item that students must describe accurately in exams.

findings.claim: Juicy Salif is described as a 'spider-like form'
findings.notes: The canonical Alessi/Starck account is that the design was sketched from the shape of a calamari squid being squeezed over a dish, not a spider. 'Spider-like' is a common lay description of its appearance, but if a student reproduced this in an exam answer it would be imprecise. The V&A and Wikipedia both refer to the squid origin story.

findings.claim: Zaha Hadid was the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize (2004)
findings.notes: Confirmed by the Pritzker Prize official website and Britannica. Year 2004 is correct; 'first woman' designation is correct.
Born 31 October 1950 in Baghdad; died 31 March 2016. Confirmed by Britannica and Pritzker Prize biography.

findings.claim: Sir Alec Issigonis (1906–1988) designed the original Mini (1959) placing the engine sideways (transverse) using front-wheel drive as a response to the Suez fuel crisis
findings.notes: Birth year 1906 and death year 1988 confirmed by Britannica. Mini launch 1959 confirmed. Transverse engine + FWD confirmed by Wikipedia (Mini article). Suez crisis (1956) as the design trigger confirmed by Wikipedia (Mini article). Lesson describes him as 'British-Greek' — Wikipedia confirms 'British automobile designer of Greek heritage', born in Smyrna (now Izmir).
Born 24 March 1834, died 3 October 1896. Confirmed by Britannica, Wikipedia, and V&A.
Born 18 January 1949. Confirmed by Britannica and Wikipedia.

findings.claim: James Dyson created 5,127 prototypes before perfecting the design
findings.notes: Confirmed by official Dyson website and multiple sources including Britannica. The figure '5,127' is Dyson's own stated count and is widely accepted.

overall_quality: TWO MEDIUM ISSUES: Juicy Salif year (1990 vs MoMA's 1988) and Louis Ghost Chair year (2002 vs Britannica/Wikipedia 2000). One LOW issue: 'spider-like' description of Juicy Salif (inspiration was a squid). All biographical dates verified correct.
